Betting by Numbers 2026 Season

Every game of the season, grouped by the day number of the date it falls on. Each game opens to both sides' numbers side by side. Games already played are shaded in the winner's color.

Worked examples

Day number. Add every digit of the date until one digit is left (a master number 11 or 22 stays as is). September 13, 2026 is 9+1+3+2+0+2+6 = 23, then 2+3 = 5. Games are grouped by that number.

Life path. The same method on a birth date. Born June 4, 1990: 6+4+1+9+9+0 = 29, then 2+9 = 11, a master number, so the life path is 11.

Name number. Each letter is worth a number (A=1, B=2 … I=9, J=1 … and so on around the alphabet); add them all and reduce. JOSH: 1+6+1+8 = 16, then 1+6 = 7.

Zodiac friends and enemies. In the Chinese zodiac each animal has traditional friends (the three signs of its trine) and traditional enemies (signs that clash with it). The count shown is how many of the tradition's links connect the two units. More friend links read as favorable, more enemy links as unfavorable.

How strong is a match? Matching numbers or friendly signs only mean the tradition says "favorable". They have not been shown to predict who wins; the scoreboard card on each game shows how often each reading was right so far.

How it's done

A field guide to numerology betting

How people try to use numbers, dates and mystical arithmetic to call sports results, written as a description of the practice. It records what bettors do and why, not what works. These ideas were tested on 3,550 games and found nothing that beat a coin flip.

1. Core foundations and calculations

Numbers from a player's name

  • Pythagorean (the most common). A–I are 1–9, J–R are 1–9, S–Z are 1–8. Add the values of every letter, then add the digits of the total until one digit is left. Example: a total of 64 becomes 6+4 = 10, then 1+0 = 1.
  • Three readings of one name. Expression uses every letter. Soul urge uses only the vowels. Personality uses only the consonants. This site shows all three for every starter.
  • Which name? Believers split on whether to use the birth name or the name on the jersey. This site uses the legal first name from the roster when it differs from the nickname, because that follows the "name given at birth" rule most numerologists state.
  • Chaldean. An older table that assigns 1–8 by sound and never uses 9. A name can reduce to a different number than it does in the Pythagorean table, and bettors pick whichever table gives the alignment they were looking for.
  • Gematria variants. English Ordinal gives A=1 through Z=26 and adds without reducing. Reverse Ordinal gives A=26 through Z=1. Other tables multiply by tens or hundreds. Section 4 covers how these are used.
  • Master numbers. 11, 22 and 33 are usually left unreduced and treated as stronger versions of 2, 4 and 6.

Numbers from a birth date: the life path

  • Reduce the month, the day and the year separately, add the three results, and reduce again. Born 1992-12-11: month 12 → 3, day 11 stays 11, year 1+9+9+2 = 21 → 3. Then 3 + 11 + 3 = 17 → 8.
  • Birthday number is just the day of the month, reduced.
  • Personal year, month and day. Personal year = birth month + birth day + the current year. Add the current month for the personal month, then the current day for the personal day. It is a number that changes every day for each person, so any player can be given a "number of the day".

Numbers from the event itself

  • Universal day number (the "event vibration"). The game date is reduced the same way. Nov 1, 2026: month 11 stays 11 (master number), day 1, year 2+0+2+6 = 10 → 1; 11 + 1 + 1 = 13 → 4. This site's day number is exactly this.
  • Time. Some bettors add the kickoff time (1:00 pm is 13:00 = 4) or the minutes into the match.
  • Location. The venue's opening year, the stadium address, the area code or ZIP code, the capacity, or the city's founding year are each reduced to a number.
  • Event name. A championship name, a Roman-numeral edition (Roman numerals are read as letters or as values), or a tournament round number can also be reduced.

Every one of these inputs is chosen by the bettor. There is no agreed rule about which date, which name or which table to use, and that freedom shapes everything in sections 2 and 5.

2. The matching methodology

The basic move: look for the same number twice

  • Player to date. A player's life path, birthday number or personal day equals the game's day number. That player is read as "in tune" with the day. This is the match the scorecard on this page marks with ★.
  • Team to date. The franchise founding date is reduced to a team life path and then treated like a birth date: the team's personal day for the game date is worked out the same way as a player's.
  • Name to date. A team or player name reduces to the same number as the date.
  • Side against side. Whichever team has more matches, or the stronger ones, is picked. A tie hands the edge to the home team, the older franchise or the team with the master number.

Softer alignments when no exact match exists

  • Number families. Many writers group 1-5-7 (independent), 2-4-8 (practical) and 3-6-9 (creative). If a number is not an exact match, it counts if it sits in the same family as the day number.
  • Own-number days. A person whose personal day equals his own life path is said to be at full strength. The scorecard marks this with ◎.
  • Coach against coach. The head coaches' life paths and personal days are compared the same way.
  • Conflict numbers. Some writers treat certain pairs as opposed, and use that to fade a team.

Numbers and the betting line

  • Founding year to spread. A team founded in 1933 might be read as 1+9+3+3 = 16 → 7, and a point spread or total containing a 7 is read as significant.
  • Date to total. The date's digits are used to pick an over/under, for example a game on the 14th with a line near 41 gets compared with 1+4 = 5.
  • Odds themselves. Prices such as +111, +777 or 3.33 are read as signs on that side.
  • Anniversaries. The last time a team won on this calendar date, or won on a date with the same number, is treated as a pattern.

Repeating numbers and cycles in futures betting

  • Angel numbers. Seeing 111, 444 or 777 repeatedly in the days before a bet is taken as a message confirming it. The bettor notices the number on a clock, a receipt or a score, and links it to the pick.
  • Season-year numbers. The year reduces to a single number (2026 → 10 → 1). Bettors back the champion whose own number matches the season's number.
  • Cycles. Nine-year and seven-year personal-year cycles are applied to teams and players. A team in a "1 year" is a rebuilding or new-start pick; a team in a "9 year" is a completion pick.
  • Historic repeats. Claims such as "the last time the calendar looked like this, this franchise won" are used to back a future champion.
  • Edition numbers. The Roman numeral of a championship game is converted and compared with team or player numbers.

The logic is always the same: pick the inputs, pick the table, look for a match, and treat the match as a signal. What changes between bettors is which inputs they allow.

3. Sport-specific applications

Football and soccer

  • Jersey numbers. A player's shirt number is matched to the date (number 23 on the 23rd) or to the day number.
  • Scoring minutes. Soccer bettors look at goal minutes (33', 77') and bet on goals in minutes that reduce to the day number.
  • Correct score and props. A final score such as 24–17 is reduced to digits and compared with the date. Anytime-scorer bets use the player whose number matches.
  • Team stats. Yards, points allowed, season win totals and records are reduced and read against the opponent's numbers.
  • Quarterbacks and coaches. In American football the quarterback and head coach are treated as the carriers of a team's number, which is why this site compares them on every game.

Basketball and baseball

  • Box-score scanning. These sports produce many numbers per game (points, rebounds, assists, hits, runs, errors), so bettors look back through past box scores for repeating digits and bet on the number to come back.
  • Player props. A player's prop line is matched to his jersey number or to the date, for example an over on 23 points on the 23rd.
  • Baseball counts. Innings, run totals, the 162-game schedule, a pitcher's career wins and the game's position in the season are all tried.
  • Long schedules. With 82 or 162 games a season, there are enough games for almost any pattern to appear and be remembered.

Horse racing and individual sports

  • Horses. The horse's name is reduced (often Chaldean), its birth or foaling date gives a life path, and the race date gives the day number. The post position, the race number on the card and the saddlecloth number are also tried.
  • Individual sports. In tennis, golf, boxing and MMA the athlete's birth date, name and ranking are matched to the tournament or fight date and the round number.
  • Combat sports. Fighter weights, ring names and the number of rounds are added to the mix.
  • Why it fits. One horse or one fighter has a single clean set of numbers, so the matching looks tidier than in a team sport with 22 starters.

4. The gematria and media-narrative angle

  • The theory. Some bettors hold that major sports results are scripted and that the script leaves clues. They calculate the gematria value of team names, headlines, event names, anniversaries and the birth dates of executives or celebrity performers, and look for the same value appearing on both sides of an event.
  • How the clue-hunting works. Typical steps: take a headline or slogan, add its letters with an Ordinal, Reverse or Reduction table, compare the totals with the date, a team's name or a past event, and then say the match shows who was "meant" to win.
  • Where the inputs come from. Team histories (founding date, previous champion years), the commissioner's or owner's birth date, halftime acts, anthem singers, and the numbering of the event.
  • Stacking. Bettors keep trying tables until one gives a match. With four or five tables and dozens of phrases, a match is close to certain.
  • What the evidence says. There is no public evidence that outcomes are scripted this way. Matches are found after the result is known, the tables are chosen to fit, and the claim cannot be wrong, since a failed match just means the wrong phrase was used. Real match-fixing has happened, but it involves money, referees or players, it leaves a trail, and investigators find it through betting patterns and communications, not headlines.

This site does not use gematria or any media-narrative method. It uses the Pythagorean name numbers and birth-date life paths described in section 1.

5. Why people gravitate to this system

  • Illusion of control. People feel more in command of chance events when they take an active part, such as choosing numbers or running a ritual. Calculating gives a random event a task the bettor can do.
  • Apophenia and pattern-seeking. The mind finds links in unrelated data. A sport that publishes thousands of numbers per week will offer a "pattern" to any reader.
  • Confirmation bias. Hits are remembered and written down. Misses are explained away ("I used the wrong table", "the coach's number was off").
  • Texas sharpshooter. The target is drawn after the shot. The bettor picks the date, name, table and number that line up with the result after it is known.
  • Too many chances. With a dozen numbers, several tables, and dates, names and stats to choose from, some match is guaranteed. Our own test found this: the one pattern that survived (life path 5) turned out to be a few strong rosters, not a number effect.
  • Subjective validation. A vague statement like "a day of new beginnings" feels accurate because it can be read to fit any outcome.
  • Selective memory and hindsight. A correct call is retold as foresight. Results from before the bet was made are treated as proof.
  • The gambler's fallacy. Believing a number is "due" is a close cousin of numerology and often appears alongside it.
  • Meaning and community. Numbers give a game a story, a feeling of insider knowledge and a shared language with other believers. For many people this is the real reward, whatever the bet does.
  • Ritual under uncertainty. When the outcome cannot be controlled, people build routines. This is common in sport itself, among athletes as well as fans.

Anyone betting real money should treat numbers like these as entertainment, not as an edge, and only stake what they can afford to lose. If gambling stops being fun, the National Council on Problem Gambling helpline is 1-800-MY-RESET.

6. Lunar cycle betting

What bettors do

  • Phase tables. Bettors look up the phase on game day (new moon, waxing crescent, first quarter, waxing gibbous, full moon, waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent) and apply a rule of thumb to it.
  • Rules of thumb. Waxing phases are said to build energy and favor high scoring and Over bets. The full moon is tied to chaos, upsets and emotional play. The new moon is tied to low scoring and defence. Eclipses and retrograde planets are sometimes added as warning days.
  • Team trends. Fans and trend accounts list teams that have lost, or won, every game in a given phase. The Lions and Thanksgiving in a waxing gibbous is the best known example.
  • The day before a full moon. A university thesis on 1978–2007 NFL games reported that the home team was understated by the point spread on that day. Its abstract calls it “possible arbitrage opportunities” and does not claim a proven strategy.
  • Player props. Some sites sell prop picks built on phases and planetary alignments, often with no published method or record.

What this site tests

  • The moon’s position is calculated for the kickoff time of every game from 1999 to 2026, not read from a phase table.
  • Each claim is checked against the real closing spread, total and moneyline, and split into years the original study covered and years it never saw.
  • Every team gets a record for each of the four standard phases (waxing and waning crescent, waxing and waning gibbous), with the full moon, new moon and day before a full moon marked separately. Open any game and choose Lunar under the deeper traditions to see them, with the posted lines where the data has them.
  • Behavioural research has not found a reliable link between the moon and human behaviour. A 1985 review of dozens of studies (Rotton and Kelly) found no significant effect, which is why any betting effect would have to come from the market’s own habits and not from the players.

Results are in the Lunar tab of any game and summarized there: the full-moon-eve effect reversed in later years, waxing gibbous showed no Over effect, and the number of “lucky” team phases was the same as with shuffled phases.
